description: Hi! I'm a student developer from Ethiopia passionate about technology, AI, and solving real-world problems. I have experience with Python, JavaScript, React, web development, and hardware projects. I'm joining NASA Space Apps to collaborate, learn, and build something meaningful. I'm looking for teammates skilled in data science, NASA data, GIS, UI/UX, agriculture, or climate science. Most importantly, I value creativity, teamwork, and curiosity. Let's build something amazing!
summary:
Fieldwise Africa is an agricultural intelligence and decision-support platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Field Shift challenge. It combines NASA Earth observation data, agricultural production records, crop calendars, and weather information to help farmers make better-informed crop-planning decisions.

The platform analyzes historical climate conditions, estimates crop yields, identifies relevant planting and harvesting periods, and provides crop recommendations based on geographic and environmental information. It integrates NASA POWER climate datasets, FAO Crop Calendar information, HarvestStat Africa, and Open-Meteo weather forecasts.

Initially focused on African agriculture, Fieldwise supports ten countries and ten major crops, with a separate experimental yield model for Ethiopian teff. Our goal is to make scientific agricultural information more accessible, support informed farming decisions, and contribute to more resilient and productive agricultural systems.
details:
Fieldwise Africa — Project Details

What does our project do?

Fieldwise Africa is a web-based agricultural intelligence and decision-support platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge.

Our project addresses the difficulty farmers face when making crop-planning decisions without sufficient access to localized climate information, historical agricultural data, and reliable crop-season information.

Fieldwise combines NASA Earth observation data, agricultural production records, crop calendars, and weather information to provide crop-yield estimates, planting and harvesting guidance, environmental insights, and crop recommendations.

The platform initially focuses on African agriculture, supporting ten countries and ten crops, including maize, sorghum, pearl millet, groundnut, cowpea, rice, cassava, sweet potato, wheat, and teff.

How does it work?

Fieldwise follows an integrated agricultural analysis workflow.

1. Geographic and Farm Information

Users provide their farming location and relevant agricultural information. The platform uses geographic coordinates, climate conditions, crop selection, and other available inputs to generate agricultural insights.

2. Climate Intelligence

NASA POWER datasets provide historical and climatological environmental information, including rainfall, temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity, and elevation.

These variables help establish the environmental context for crop analysis.

3. Crop Yield Estimation

Our regional crop-yield model uses HarvestStat Africa v1.2 agricultural production records combined with historical NASA POWER climate information.

We developed a standardized Ridge Regression model to estimate regional crop yields across ten African countries and ten crops.

We also developed a separate experimental Ethiopian teff yield model using agricultural research-trial records combined with NASA POWER climatology.

4. Planting and Harvest Calendar

The platform integrates the FAO Crop Calendar API to identify suggested crop planting and harvesting windows.

It considers available country, crop, and agro-ecological-zone information. When FAO calendar information is unavailable, the system can fall back to historical HarvestStat crop-season records.

5. Crop Recommendations and Planning

The backend evaluates supported crops using environmental inputs, estimated yields, and available planting-calendar information.

It considers whether a suggested planting window is currently open and helps users explore suitable crop options and their seasonal context.

6. Weather Forecasting

Open-Meteo provides current weather conditions and a 14-day forecast through a separate weather service, helping users understand near-term weather conditions alongside historical climate information.

Datasets and scientific resources

Our project combines several scientific and agricultural data sources:

NASA Earth Observation

  • NASA POWER Climatology API: Long-term climate information.
  • NASA POWER Temporal API: Historical climate observations over time.
  • NASA POWER Monthly API: Monthly climate information.
  • NASA-USDA soil-moisture reference: Additional soil-water context.

Agricultural and Crop Information

  • FAO Crop Calendar and FAO Crop Calendar API: Suggested planting and harvesting periods.
  • HarvestStat Africa v1.2: Historical agricultural production, harvested area, crop yields, and crop-season records.
  • FAOSTAT yield reference: Complementary agricultural production and yield information.

Weather Information

  • Open-Meteo: Current weather conditions and short-term forecasts.

These sources provide complementary information. Historical climate, current weather, long-term climatology, crop-season records, and agricultural production statistics are treated as different types of evidence rather than interchangeable measurements.

Machine Learning and Agricultural Intelligence

Fieldwise includes two separate experimental crop-yield models.

Regional crop-yield model

The regional model uses HarvestStat Africa v1.2 and NASA POWER historical climate features. It applies standardized Ridge Regression with crop-specific climate interactions.

The training dataset contains 1,607 joined country-crop-year records across ten African countries, covering 1984–2024.

The model was evaluated using a chronological holdout of later years. Its reported evaluation metrics are MAE of approximately 1.68 tonnes/hectare, RMSE of approximately 2.90 tonnes/hectare, and R² of approximately 0.776.

These metrics describe evaluation on regional historical records, not verified accuracy for individual farms.

Experimental Ethiopian teff model

We also developed a separate teff yield model using 382 eligible Ethiopian agricultural research-trial records from an open research dataset. It combines trial information, soil properties, fertilizer application, and NASA POWER climate features.

This model was evaluated using held-out locations and remains experimental because the research dataset is relatively small and does not represent every Ethiopian farm.

Technologies and tools

Our current implementation uses:

  • Python for data processing and machine learning.
  • FastAPI for backend APIs.
  • Pandas and NumPy for data analysis and processing.
  • Scikit-learn-style regression methodology implemented in the model training pipeline.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the web application.
  • SQLite for backend saved-plan storage.
  • JSON and CSV for datasets and trained model artifacts.
  • Render configuration for backend deployment.

Benefits and intended impact

Fieldwise aims to make agricultural information more accessible and useful by:

  • Translating NASA climate information into understandable agricultural insights.
  • Helping farmers explore crop options and estimated yields.
  • Providing planting and harvesting guidance based on available agricultural calendars.
  • Combining historical agricultural production with environmental information.
  • Supporting better-informed seasonal crop planning.
  • Making agricultural data more accessible across African regions.

Our long-term goal is to support more informed, climate-aware agricultural decisions, particularly in regions where access to scientific agricultural information is limited.

Creativity and innovation

The creativity behind Fieldwise is its integration of multiple scientific and agricultural information sources into one decision-support experience.

Instead of presenting satellite data, climate charts, crop calendars, and agricultural statistics as disconnected resources, we connect them through a common workflow.

Our regional crop-yield model, separate Ethiopian teff research model, FAO calendar integration, and weather forecasting provide complementary perspectives for agricultural planning.

We also prioritize transparency by communicating data sources, geographic limitations, missing information, and the uncertainty associated with modeled estimates.

Factors considered during development

Our team considered scientific accuracy, dataset availability, geographic coverage, crop characteristics, usability, and the differences between regional estimates and actual farm conditions.

We also considered that historical climate data cannot replace live weather information, crop calendars are not rainfall forecasts, and regional yield estimates should not be interpreted as guaranteed farm-level outcomes.

Fieldwise is designed as a decision-support platform that helps farmers and agricultural advisors explore evidence and make more informed decisions, rather than replacing local agricultural expertise.
